following-100.intro: Gary E. Stevenson remembered visiting farm stands with his family as a child. One stand was especially known for a particular fruit.
following-100.text: As a child, Gary E. Stevenson visited farm stands with his family for fresh fruit. One stand was known for its delicious peaches. He used tasting fruit as an illustration: hearing someone describe gospel truth is different from discovering it by living it.
following-100.takeaway: We discover the sweetness of the gospel by living it ourselves.
following-100.context: Living the gospel helps us learn for ourselves; it does not mean every day will feel easy.

following-200.intro: A homesick missionary wanted to go home. After encouragement from Christian C. Chigbundu, he and his trainer made a plan. A later letter described a change in his experience.
following-200.text: A new missionary was crying and wanted to go home. Christian C. Chigbundu encouraged him, and the missionary made a scripture-study plan with his trainer, especially studying the Book of Mormon. Later, he wrote that he understood his purpose, felt happier, and wanted to stay.
following-200.takeaway: Studying the scriptures can strengthen our faith, help us understand our purpose, and give us strength to keep serving.
following-200.context: This is one missionary's experience. It does not set a timetable for overcoming distress.

following-300.intro: As a young missionary, David O. McKay noticed an inscription above a doorway: WHAT E'ER THOU ART ACT WELL THY PART. Quentin L. Cook recalled how those words changed McKay's approach to his responsibilities.
following-300.text: As a young missionary, David O. McKay noticed a message carved above a doorway: WHAT E'ER THOU ART ACT WELL THY PART. It helped him resolve to do his best in every responsibility. Quentin L. Cook used that experience to teach integrity and lifelong discipleship.
following-300.takeaway: Follow Christ with integrity by doing your best in every responsibility, including the small ones.
following-300.context: The school-project situation in the question is an application of this lesson.

following-400.intro: A woman faithfully paid tithing but was disappointed when the promotion and salary increase she hoped for did not arrive. Moisés Villanueva invited her to reconsider what she expected from obedience.
following-400.text: A woman faithfully paid a full tithe but did not receive the job promotion and salary increase she hoped for. Her testimony of tithing weakened. Moisés Villanueva invited her to notice significant but subtle blessings, drawing on his own reflection with help from the Holy Ghost. The story does not report a later promotion.
following-400.takeaway: Trust God's way and timing, and recognize His significant but sometimes subtle blessings.
following-400.context: Obedience does not guarantee a particular worldly result or our preferred timetable. Acknowledge disappointment honestly.

following-500.intro: James G. O. Fantone accidentally wrote his own name on his daughter's school form, then corrected it by adding her first name. That simple correction led him to reflect on what it means to take Christ's name.
following-500.text: When filling out his daughter's school form, James G. O. Fantone wrote his own name instead of hers. Adding her first name fixed the mistake. Taking Christ's name is a much deeper commitment: becoming like Him through covenant and an ongoing determination to serve Him, especially by serving other people.
following-500.takeaway: Taking Christ's name means becoming like Him through an ongoing commitment to serve Him and other people.
following-500.context: Adding a name as a label is different from living a covenant. Youth can apply this through ordinary, practical service.

identity-100.intro: Hutch U. Fale gathered baby pictures of his children for a family conversation. He used those pictures to help them understand how Heavenly Father feels about them.
identity-100.text: Hutch U. Fale gathered baby pictures of his children and asked what they had done as babies to earn their parents' love. They had done nothing. Their parents already loved them. He used that love to help explain our worth as children of God.
identity-100.takeaway: You are a beloved child of Heavenly Parents. Your worth and Their love are already yours.
identity-100.context: Worth and being loved do not require perfection.

identity-200.intro: Rosemary K. Chibota's daughter reminded her of a Southern African greeting meaning I see you. Chibota used it to teach how we can treat other people.
identity-200.text: Rosemary K. Chibota's daughter reminded her of a Southern African greeting meaning I see you. The greeting communicates more than hello: recognition, respect, human worth, concern, and belonging. It tells a person that they matter.
identity-200.takeaway: Seeing people as children of God helps us recognize their worth and treat them with respect and belonging.
identity-200.context: Use the greeting's meaning here; the supplied captions do not reliably preserve its original spelling.

identity-300.intro: Andrea Muñoz Spannaus's navigation app confused a freeway with a parallel street. She called her husband, who could guide her once he understood her actual location. She connected the experience with the Lord's knowledge of us.
identity-300.text: Andrea Muñoz Spannaus's navigation app confused the freeway she was on with a parallel street. She exited and called her husband. Once he knew her actual location, he could guide her. She explained that the Lord already knows our real circumstances, weaknesses, and questions—and that knowing them does not make Him love us less.
identity-300.takeaway: The Lord knows exactly where you are, including your questions and weaknesses, and He still loves you.
identity-300.context: Our weaknesses do not remove our worth or the Lord's love.

identity-400.intro: Dale G. Renlund's sister Linda read scriptural promises as if an asterisk applied to her personally. She struggled with the feeling that those promises were for other people.
identity-400.text: Dale G. Renlund's sister Linda read promises in scripture as if each carried an asterisk excluding her personally. She came to understand that she was included in God's promises too. Her lesson challenged the idea that everyone else could receive His promised blessings except her.
identity-400.takeaway: God's promises include you. Trust Jesus Christ and your covenant relationship with Him rather than imagining a personal exclusion.
identity-400.context: Keep the conditions of a promise and God's timing with the encouragement; do not promise an instant result.

identity-500.intro: A young man asked Jesus about eternal life. Andrea Muñoz Spannaus drew attention to Christ's first response to him, before His invitation to improve.
identity-500.text: A young man asked Jesus about eternal life. Andrea Muñoz Spannaus emphasized the order of Christ's response: He looked at the young man with love before inviting him to improve. The invitation to grow came from love, not from a judgment that he had no worth.
identity-500.takeaway: Christ loves us as we are and invites us to grow. His invitation to improve begins with love.
identity-500.context: Affirm worth while encouraging repentance, repair, and a constructive next step.

revelation-100.intro: After receiving a life-changing calling, Gérald Caussé prayed for guidance. An ordinary moment at home led him to a scripture that reassured him.
revelation-100.text: After receiving a life-changing calling, Gérald Caussé prayed for guidance. He felt prompted to open a Church magazine on his kitchen table. A scripture he found there reassured him about bearing witness of Christ.
revelation-100.takeaway: Seek the Lord in prayer and respond to the Spirit's promptings. He can reassure and guide you as you serve Him.
revelation-100.context: This is his reported experience; guidance does not always arrive in the same way.

revelation-200.intro: Timothy L. Farnes was reading at an airport near an anxious missionary. A prompting interrupted his reading and changed what he did next.
revelation-200.text: At an airport, Timothy L. Farnes was reading when he felt prompted to look again at an anxious missionary. He asked whether the missionary was okay. He and his wife helped him navigate flying alone, and later escorted him to his mission leaders.
revelation-200.takeaway: Act on promptings to notice people and help them. Ordinary encounters can become opportunities to minister like Christ.
revelation-200.context: His response included practical help and companionship, rather than a promise that fear would instantly disappear.

revelation-300.intro: Patrick Kearon learned to fly a glider as a teenager. Unseen air could carry it upward or downward, and his training taught him to notice what was happening and respond. He later compared gliding with receiving spiritual guidance.
revelation-300.text: As a teenager learning to fly a glider, Patrick Kearon needed a trained guide and learned to notice cues from unseen rising air. When he recognized lift, he could turn into it and stay with it; he also learned to turn away from sinking air. Later, he connected those learned responses with spiritual practices and guidance.
revelation-300.takeaway: Learn to recognize and respond to spiritual lift through Christ's grace and the Holy Spirit. Follow faithful guidance and turn away from influences that pull you down.
revelation-300.context: The glider is an analogy. A spiritual application should include seeking, attending to guidance, and acting faithfully.

revelation-400.intro: After a disagreement early in his marriage, Thabo Lebethoa recalled something he had previously learned. It helped him decide how to address the challenge; the account does not describe his exact reconciliation steps.
revelation-400.text: After an argument early in his marriage, Thabo Lebethoa remembered Christ's scriptural teaching against contention. His mind was enlightened, and he knew how to address the challenge. The account does not describe the exact steps he took to reconcile.
revelation-400.takeaway: Consistent scripture study prepares us to receive Christ's light and guidance when everyday challenges arise.
revelation-400.context: Pausing, apologizing, or listening are possible applications, rather than reported details of his response.

revelation-500.intro: Clark G. Gilbert visited a home where five people had different concerns. Even though time was short, he felt a prompting about what he should do before teaching them.
revelation-500.text: Clark G. Gilbert visited a home where five people had different concerns. Even with limited time, he felt prompted to wait instead of interrupting. He listened, came to understand them, and later taught from love. Following a prompting meant restraint before speaking.
revelation-500.takeaway: Responding to the Spirit can mean waiting and listening. Understanding people helps us speak truth with love.
revelation-500.context: Listening and responding thoughtfully can be a faithful action.

hope-100.intro: Dale G. Renlund described a patient recovering from two transplants. After a remarkable recovery, the patient had two complaints about breakfast. Recovery was still exhausting.
hope-100.text: After two transplants and a remarkable recovery, a patient was bothered that the oatmeal was not hot and the milk was not cold. Dale G. Renlund acknowledged the exhaustion involved in recovery while using the experience to teach remembering the bigger picture and God's mercies.
hope-100.takeaway: Remember the bigger picture: how God has helped you and what He has promised. That perspective can strengthen your trust when today's difficulties loom large.
hope-100.context: Renlund acknowledges the patient's exhausted coping capacity. Remembering blessings does not dismiss legitimate suffering.

hope-200.intro: While traveling to begin mission service, Kevin J. Hathaway's family faced a frightening crash when loose tires struck their cars. He described how they were supported through the difficulties that followed.
hope-200.text: While traveling to begin mission service, Kevin J. Hathaway's family faced a frightening crash when loose tires struck their cars. They received peace and assurance from the Spirit, as well as practical assistance from other people. They arrived without serious injury after working through the difficulties.
hope-200.takeaway: Seek Jesus Christ in difficulty. His peace, enabling grace, and help through other people can sustain us as we work through challenges.
hope-200.context: Receiving peace and help does not mean every problem is immediately fixed.

hope-300.intro: Tamara W. Runia's grandson Jack was asked what he would do if a Lego building set had no picture of the finished model on its box. He said he would still be willing to follow the instructions.
hope-300.text: Tamara W. Runia's grandson Jack shared a lesson prepared with his father. When asked what he would do if a Lego building set had no picture of the finished model on the box, he said he could still follow the instructions because he trusted the designer. She connected that trust with continuing in faith without seeing the complete plan.
hope-300.takeaway: Trust God enough to take the next faithful step, even when you cannot see His complete plan.
hope-300.context: The missing box picture is a what-if illustration, rather than a reported package he received.

hope-400.intro: Tamara W. Runia's brother struggled to finish a sculpture of his own likeness. After initially refusing help, he allowed a skilled instructor to work on it. The finished sculpture still looked like him.
hope-400.text: Tamara W. Runia's brother tried to sculpt his own likeness but could not make the eyes lifelike. At first he refused help, then humbly asked a skilled instructor. The instructor carved more deeply and shaped what the student could not, while the sculpture remained uniquely the student's. She connected receiving that help with receiving Christ's help to grow.
hope-400.takeaway: Humbly receive Christ's help. He can shape and strengthen us beyond what we can accomplish alone.
hope-400.context: The analogy does not explain the cause of every painful event or promise that desired outcomes arrive quickly.

hope-500.intro: Ninety miles into a hundred-mile race, Michael A. Dunn nearly quit. Ted accompanied him through the last ten miles. A later photograph revealed another way Ted had been helping without shortening the race.
hope-500.text: Ninety miles into a hundred-mile race, Michael A. Dunn nearly quit. Ted encouraged him and stayed patiently beside him. Ted also quietly carried Dunn's pack and water; a later photograph revealed that help. The route was not shortened, but Dunn did not have to face its last ten miles alone.
hope-500.takeaway: Christ can strengthen us and send people to help carry our burdens while the course remains difficult. We can offer that same practical care and encouragement to others.
hope-500.context: Help can include emotional support and practical action while the challenge remains.

covenants-100.intro: Dieter F. Uchtdorf and his wife celebrated an important choice made by two of their great-grandchildren. It was a step in their covenant journey.
covenants-100.text: Dieter F. Uchtdorf and his wife rejoiced when two of their great-grandchildren chose baptism. He connected these individual covenant choices with the examples and support of family and friends.
covenants-100.takeaway: Baptism begins a covenant relationship with Christ and brings us into a people who support and care for one another.
covenants-100.context: Making a covenant begins an ongoing relationship and commitment.

covenants-200.intro: Members apologized to Gerrit W. Gong that their temple building was small. His reply redirected their attention to what makes a temple important.
covenants-200.text: Members apologized to Gerrit W. Gong that their temple building was small. He responded that ordinances and covenants are not big or small. The spiritual blessings of temple worship are not measured by a building's size.
covenants-200.takeaway: Temple blessings come through sacred ordinances and covenants with God, whatever the size of the building.
covenants-200.context: Spiritual blessings are not a competition between temple buildings.

covenants-300.intro: Gerrit W. Gong described children of modest means who saved for a gift their mother had requested. She cherished it through years of temple service.
covenants-300.text: Children of modest means saved to buy their mother her own temple clothing, something she had requested. She cherished the gift through years of temple service. Gerrit W. Gong shared their practical sacrifice and loving support for her worship.
covenants-300.takeaway: Loving sacrifice and practical support can help our families worship in the temple and honor their covenants.
covenants-300.context: Apply this through support appropriate to a person's age, means, and circumstances.

covenants-400.intro: Ciro Schmeil recalled Haggai speaking to people busy with their own houses while the Lord's house lay unfinished. Haggai told them to consider their ways, comparing their efforts to putting wages into a bag with holes. Schmeil connected their response with something we are asked to build today.
covenants-400.takeaway: Make your relationship with Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ a priority by adjusting your life to make and keep covenants.
covenants-400.text: In Haggai's account, the people had neglected rebuilding the temple. They reconsidered their priorities, repented, and began rebuilding. Ciro Schmeil connected that change with what we are asked to build today: a strong relationship with Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ through making and keeping covenants.
covenants-400.context: The present-day application concerns a covenant relationship with God.

covenants-500.intro: David A. Bednar described an imagined traveler refused entry with a valid but damaged passport. He compared travel documents with spiritual credentials, explaining both the analogy's meaning and an important limit.
covenants-500.text: David A. Bednar described an illustrative traveler refused entry with a valid but damaged passport. Receiving credentials and continuing to care for them both mattered. An authorized stamp supplied a verifying witness. He used the comparison to teach ongoing covenant faithfulness and the Holy Spirit of Promise. He explicitly stated its limit: hardships and injuries suffered through no fault of our own do not invalidate covenants or God's promises.
covenants-500.takeaway: Keep honoring your covenants with Christ. Hardship suffered through no fault of your own does not cancel those covenants or God's promises.
covenants-500.context: Keep the adversity qualification with the analogy. Ratification is usually over time as people repent and honor covenants.

serving-100.intro: During a Primary program, a boy got caught up in a problem with his clothing. Paul H. Sinclair noticed how another child responded when the boy could not free himself.
serving-100.text: During a Primary program, a boy had buttoned his sleeve to his lapel and could not move freely. A girl beside him unbuttoned it so he could move again. Paul H. Sinclair, who had felt irritated, learned through the Holy Ghost to help before judging.
serving-100.takeaway: Be quick to help and slow to judge. Small, compassionate actions can show the Savior's love.
serving-100.context: A small, practical act can express Christ's love.

serving-200.intro: Gabriel W. Reid remembered outdoor Primary classes under a mango tree. Years later, particular things about his teachers still stood out to him.
serving-200.text: Gabriel W. Reid remembered Primary classes held outside under a mango tree. What stayed with him was his teachers' love. They knew the children personally and by name, helping them feel the Savior's love.
serving-200.takeaway: Love the people you teach and know them personally. That care helps them feel Christ's love.
serving-200.context: Personal attention and recognition mattered more than an elaborate setting.

serving-300.intro: A school janitor thanked Rosemary K. Chibota and her husband because of how their daughter treated him. Her everyday actions had made an impression.
serving-300.text: A school janitor thanked Rosemary K. Chibota and her husband because their daughter saw him as a person. She greeted him, knew his name, and helped clean after lunch. Those ordinary actions offered recognition, dignity, and practical care.
serving-300.takeaway: See people as beloved children of God, then show it through personal recognition and useful service.
serving-300.context: Seeing a person's worth can lead to specific, useful service.

serving-400.intro: Timothy L. Farnes felt unappreciated after his question was dismissed at a leadership meeting. He wanted to skip ward temple night, but his wife encouraged him to go. In the temple dressing room, Dallin H. Oaks asked how he was doing. Farnes forced a smile and said everything was great; after he changed, Oaks was still waiting and asked how he was really doing.
serving-400.takeaway: Minister like Christ by seeing the person, showing compassion, and acting. Taking time to listen can help someone feel loved and ready to keep serving.
serving-400.text: Timothy L. Farnes was discouraged after a meeting and reluctantly went to the temple at his wife's encouragement. Dallin H. Oaks noticed him and asked how he was doing. When Farnes gave a forced smile, a second question—how he was really doing—made room for honesty. Oaks listened, appreciated him, encouraged him, and offered an embrace.
serving-400.context: The lesson is attentive care. An application should respect a person's comfort and boundaries.

serving-500.intro: Clark G. Gilbert answered a friend's criticism of the Church with an angry retort. Although he seemed to win the debate, he later regretted his response.
serving-500.text: When a friend criticized the Church, Clark G. Gilbert answered with an angry retort. Later he realized that winning the debate had cost him the Spirit and had not helped his friend. He learned that holding a conviction and caring about the person must go together.
serving-500.takeaway: Stand for truth with charity. Help the person and keep the Spirit by speaking with love and listening to understand.
serving-500.context: A respectful response can communicate a conviction without insult, shame, or abandoning the relationship.
